compute.body: Semiconductor and electronic-component output growth accelerated materially to 19.9%, while capacity utilization rose to 76.5%. Computer and peripheral-equipment output growth slowed materially to 6.5%, and utilization edged down to 81.3%. Both segments are still expanding, but the latest acceleration is concentrated in semiconductors.
compute.headline: Semiconductor production accelerates as computer-equipment growth cools

data_center.body: Available records list 1,556 sites in development, equal to 0.51 times the 3,068 operating sites, and separately track 894 active pipeline sites. Data Center Dynamics reported that Amazon withdrew its application for a data-center campus at the GWU site in Ashburn, Virginia. A single withdrawal does not establish a broad contraction, but it illustrates why project counts should not be treated as completed capacity.
data_center.headline: Amazon’s Ashburn withdrawal illustrates project attrition alongside a large pipeline

finance.body: The Chicago Fed NFCI stands at -0.50 after rising 0.03 over three months. Lender strain edged up to 16.0, while borrower strain is 26.0. CNBC reported that CoreWeave credit-default swaps reached distress levels, and Morningstar reported declines in CoreWeave and data-center bonds over debt and capital-spending concerns. Those reports identify pressure in particular AI-linked credits, but they do not show that the same stress applies across borrowers or the financial system.
finance.headline: The NFCI edges higher as reports flag CoreWeave credit stress

grid_storage.body: The active interconnection queue remains 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% is at executed-agreement or construction stages. Storage accounts for 552.7 GW, and only 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. Utility Dive reported that FERC rejected most of PJM’s large-load interconnection plan, days after PJM approved fast-track interconnection for 2.1 GW from Engie and LS Power. Individual projects can advance even while rules for larger-load connections remain unsettled; the decisions do not alter the low historical conversion rate.
grid_storage.headline: Selective PJM decisions leave the broader queue constraint intact

macro.body: Public-equity measures improved. The AI Equity Index edged up to 31.8, the median one-year return rose materially to 13.6%, and 61.3% of covered companies now have positive one-year returns. Credit signals are less uniform: the Chicago Fed NFCI is -0.50 after a 0.03 rise over three months, while CNBC reported distress-level pricing in CoreWeave credit-default swaps and Morningstar reported declines in CoreWeave and data-center bonds over debt and capital-spending concerns. The contrast is between broader equity gains and pressure in specific AI-infrastructure credits, rather than a single market-wide direction. The physical project pipeline remains large. Available records show 1,556 data-center sites in development, about half the 3,068 operating sites, and separately track 894 active pipeline sites. Data Center Dynamics also reported that Amazon withdrew its application for a campus in Ashburn, Virginia. The withdrawal is one instance rather than evidence of a broad slowdown, but it reinforces the distinction between a listed project and completed capacity. Power remains central to converting that pipeline into operating capacity. Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.1%, ahead of 1.2% growth in total retail demand, and net planned generation additions total 225.2 GW. Separately, 2,061 GW remains in active interconnection queues, only 24.2% of it at executed-agreement or construction stages; just 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. Utility Dive’s report of a 960-MW Indiana nuclear pact among AEP, Amazon, and X-energy shows continued efforts to secure supply, but a pact and a project pipeline are not operating generation. Downstream evidence is improving slowly. Current business AI use edged up to 24.6%, while 28.6% of businesses expect use within six months. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth, with power and communication construction leading at 0.8%. Nonfarm-business productivity and real output are growing 2.2% and 2.5%, respectively, but median real weekly earnings growth is only 0.1%. These aggregate measures do not isolate AI’s contribution, and the evidence for organizational deployment remains clearer than the evidence for broadly distributed labor gains.
macro.headline: Equity breadth improves, but infrastructure delivery and broad economic gains remain uneven

market.body: The AI Equity Index edged up to 31.8, while the median one-year return rose materially to 13.6%. The share of covered companies with positive one-year returns also increased slightly to 61.3%, and average sector trading pressure eased to 47.9. Most covered companies are now positive over one year, although the improvement in breadth remains incremental.
market.headline: AI equity breadth improves as the median return rises

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

paragraphs.text: Equity performance has become less even. The AI Equity Index rose slightly to 32.1, yet the median one-year return fell materially to 10.3% and positive-return breadth slipped to 60.8%. Operating cash flow still covers current CapEx 1.39 times, but that ratio and cash-reserve coverage of 0.92 years both edged down, while borrower strain rose to 26.0. Forward commitments stand at 4.74 times current CapEx. The Financial Times also reported a surge in default-insurance trading amid AI debt worries. These are signs of narrower cushions and greater credit concern, but they do not by themselves establish a broad funding break.

Physical expansion remains substantial. Semiconductor and electronic-component output is growing 19.9%, compared with 6.5% for computer and peripheral equipment. Data-center records list 1,556 development sites against 3,068 operating sites and separately track 894 active pipeline sites. These indicators combine realized manufacturing growth with a large inventory of planned facilities rather than providing a direct measure of delivered computing capacity. The Texas Tribune’s report that TCEQ shut down its permit-filing system amid a data-center dispute adds uncertainty around permitting, but one shutdown does not establish a broader slowdown.

The grid remains the clearest gap between scale and readiness. The active interconnection queue totals 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% has reached an executed agreement or construction. Operating storage has a weighted average duration of 2.8 hours, and 45.5% of capacity can run for at least four hours, with both measures edging lower. RTO Insider’s report of lukewarm stakeholder support for NYISO’s large-load interconnection framework indicates that connection rules remain unsettled. The buildout therefore has substantial industrial momentum, but much of the power infrastructure required to support new large loads remains at an early stage.
